tree.intro: Let's walk through King's Pawn vs Sicilian Defense — White plays the King's Pawn, Black answers with the Sicilian Defense. Watch how they meet.
tree.outro: That's how King's Pawn vs Sicilian Defense plays out.

node.idea: We take White and meet the Sicilian — today we play normal theory, then deliberately sacrifice a piece and show how to fight back from a lost position.
We open the Alapin with c3.

The knight to c6 is one of the most common responses, but it's already a serious inaccuracy — not quite a mistake if Black follows up correctly, but one more slip and things get disastrously bad within five or six moves.

We play the bishop to g5 — a believable blunder, and at least it develops a piece. The comedy would be if Black declined it.

We even offer the bishop to a6 — all but begging Black to win material; it's oddly hard to give a piece away.
Black takes on c3 with check.
We recapture, bxc3.

Black wins our bishop, the pawn recapturing on a6 — the sacrifice is complete, and we've even traded off another pair of minors, making it harder on ourselves. Now the recovery begins, a full piece down. First, know this: ...e5 does not win the knight back — after ...h6, the bishop to h4, ...g5 unpins, and if the bishop drops to g3 the knight is free. Basic, but essential.
So we play e5 — in a situation like this it's a genuine attempt to complicate the game.

Black plays h6. It slightly weakens his structure, but down a piece a small weakness isn't enough — we need something concrete. The idea is to take on f6: after ...hxg5 we push to g7, and even after ...Rg8 we defend the g7-pawn indirectly with the queen to h5 — if the rook grabs g7, the queen forks on h8. Recovery rarely comes in a single move: build tension and sow doubt.
We capture on f6.
Black wins our bishop, recapturing on g5.

We push to g7 and set the queen toward h5, sowing doubt. This game is really about recovery technique when you're lost, and the principles are these. Complicate — pose your opponent decision after decision, because decisions breed fatigue and doubt. Keep your pieces active — bring the rook in with h4 rather than a timid g3, and ask the "Shankland question": what happens if you just do it anyway, developing and ignoring a pawn? Defend key pawns by developing, not by a passive king move — a rook to d3 both guards c3 and prepares to lift to g3. Manoeuvre the knight toward a dream square like d6, via f7. Use a break like d5 not only to lure the bishop off b7 but to open lines and strip away defenders. And once you win material back, convert with a passed pawn — push it hard while the opponent is passive, escort it with a rook cutting off the king, and finish with the ladder-mate technique, bringing your own king up to guard the checking square so the rooks can deliver mate. Even dead lost, purposeful, problem-posing play saves a remarkable number of games.

node.idea: We face d5, the direct counter in the centre.

The queen recaptures on d5, and we play d4 — a highly theoretical position we've had many times.
The knight to f6, the main move.
We develop our own knight to f3 — all theory. Black is at a major crossroads with four or so worthy options.

The knight to c6 — the natural move if you're seeing this for the first time. Its drawback: the f8-bishop stays locked behind the e7 pawn. The course's best way to punish it exploits exactly that: after d takes c5, Black can't recapture on c5 with the bishop, so the queen must take, handing White tempi. So the move is d takes c5.
We take, capturing on c5 — you might be reluctant, since it lets Black trade queens and drive our king out for a pawn, and you might think c5 is easy to win back, but that's far from true.
The queen takes d1 with check, and our king recaptures on d1 — if he knows the theory, this gets sharp.

a5, a very understandable move preventing b4 — but that doesn't mean we must part with the c5 pawn. We have many ways to cling to it, though not at the cost of our position. The bishop to e3 runs into the knight to g4, ruining our structure; h3 to meet e6 with the bishop to e3 runs into the knight to d5; and a3 with b4 fails to a takes b4, c takes b4, the knight takes b4. So a more indirect approach — a5 weakens the b5 square.

The bishop to b5 has limited value since Black plays e6, so I like the Alapin-esque idea of getting the knight to b5. So the knight to a3 — from b5 the knight eyes c7, and if Black pushes the e-pawn and we play the knight to b5, we can even reach d6, where after Black takes and we recapture, we get the bishop pair and dark-square control; even if Black wins the pawn back, we'd get the better endgame. A nice flexible developing move, waiting for Black to show his cards.

It may seem like one-move-itis, but it's a serious threat: to stop the knight to c7, Black must ruin his king safety by moving the king to the d-file, or lose queenside castling by moving the rook — either way a wasted move. The king to d8.

Now our knight on b5 just chills. We could also go from the other side with the knight to g5 — sticking knights on b5 and g5, hitting f7 and c7. Black would play g6 to defend f7, and after f4 Black could counter with h6. Or the straightforward bishop to c4, simple and strong. The knight to g5 is the move to win on the spot — I'm going for the throat, and it's not a big commitment: knights move backwards.

The bishop to e6 immediately justifies the knight to g5, because we have the standing option of taking on e6 and permanently wrecking Black's structure — I'll take those doubled pawns any day. You don't have to take immediately, but not having to rush a move doesn't mean you shouldn't play it.

I don't see a reason to keep the knight there, so let's take on e6 while we can. Now the e6 pawn is one of Black's main weaknesses — we could hit it with a rook to e1, but I see a more effective, unconventional development: getting the bishop to h3 or g4, either via the bishop to e2 and g4, or g3 and the bishop to h3, which I call the hyper-fianchetto.
I like g3 — it's a bit more elegant.
We follow up with our plan, the bishop to h3.

e5 — its obvious drawback is that the d5-knight loses its support. The idea plays itself: we want a rook on d1, not to attack the knight in some random way; if the bishop to b6, the knight drops to c7 and we've achieved nothing.

So instead we move the king off d1 — to the c-file or e-file, doesn't matter; I like keeping the king central in the endgame. The king to e2. Notice how our pawns restrict both black knights — d4, b4 and f4 are all covered, a major appeal of g3 over the bishop-e2 route. Now the devastating threat of the rook to d1, and Black is borderline dead lost — not just from the extra pawn, but because his position is in shambles. He can't castle, the king has moved; against the rook to d1 there's no good answer — if the king to e8, the rook to d1, and if the rook to d8 defends the knight, we play the rook takes d5, the classic trick with the knight coming to c7 to win the rook. e6 might be the only move for breathing room, but then we take on e6 and Black can resign. What's wrong with the knight to f6? A check on d1 forces the king to e8 — which is partly why we put the bishop on h3: not just to hit e6, but so that when Black played e5 we also contained the king, preventing it from reaching c8.

node.idea: d4 already. This is an anti-Sicilian move — the entry point into the Smith-Morra Gambit, where White throws a pawn at us to rip the position open.
We take, capturing on d4. Now White has a choice — recapture, or slip into an open Sicilian with a knight to f3.
c3 — the true Morra pawn offer. Here there's almost an ideological choice: grab the pawn and play right into a Morra player's dream, or refuse it and take the fun out of White's whole setup.
The knight to f6 is that refusal. We won't touch the c3 pawn — that's exactly what Morra specialists want. Instead we hit e4 and steer the game somewhere White is far less prepared for.
e5 lunges forward, kicking our knight. This is the transposition we were after — the pawn structure is now an Alapin, not a gambit.

The knight settles on d5, and we've reached an Alapin Sicilian by force. This is the whole point: instead of memorizing forcing Morra theory where one slip loses in five moves, we've reached a much safer, more understandable structure.

White recaptures on d4, rebuilding the center. The beauty of this whole line is that you can play it without fear — you don't have to know it to the same razor's-edge depth the accepted Morra demands.
d6 immediately, chipping away at White's advanced center. We start questioning that e5 spearhead right away rather than letting White sit comfortably.
A knight to f3 develops and props up e5. Now we have several tries — we could grab on e5 — but the cleanest is the main road.

The knight to c6 is the main, principled continuation, piling on d4 and finishing our development. Against the standard bishop to c4 there's a rare line — one Sam Shankland showed me — that really tests how deep our opponent's theory runs.
But White plays the bishop to d3 instead of c4. The pause before it tells us they're already out of book — this is just a developing move, nothing special, and crucially it doesn't do what c4 would.

So we develop the bishop to g4, eyeing the f3 knight. If White does bail out by capturing on d6, we recapture with the queen and land an ideal isolated-queen's-pawn setup, with our knight already planted on the blockading square in front of that pawn.

White does go queen to b3, we chop on f3, White recaptures with the g-pawn, and we commit to e6. Now the sharp line is queen takes b7, knight takes d4, and the check on b5 has to be reckoned with — we capture the bishop, White checks with the queen from b5, and the point I'd missed at first is that we don't have to run the king to e7; we simply block with the queen to d7, and the resulting endgame favors us because White's pawn structure is a wreck. In the game White actually declines the b7 pawn, which makes our path obvious — keep striking at the center with a capture on e5 while White still can't finish developing. The safe alternatives, a rook to b8 or the queen to d7, were both excellent; honestly the queen to d7 would have been far easier to handle. But we're playing maximally principled, trusting the complications, because our lead in development is enormous and White's whole position is on the verge of collapse.

Our knight is hanging and can't move — a retreat walks into a bishop check on b5 that's mating, and the knight on c6 will be under crushing fire. So the near-automatic move is the bishop check on b4, played essentially without further calculation, because it can only help us: it opens the door to castle kingside — a safety valve, a worst-case escape. Even in the grimmest scenario we could sacrifice the knight on c6, throw a rook to c8 with tempo, and dream of infiltrating on c1 after a knight takes c3. That's all brainstorming, not forced yet.

White blocks with the bishop to d2. The first question I ask is simply: can we castle? If yes, most of our problems dissolve and we never have to shuffle the king to f8. And there's a gorgeous resource lurking — after we castle and White grabs on c6, a rook to c8 sets up a rook lift to c1 with check that isn't a blunder, because the blocking bishop on d2 is pinned. When the king steps to e2 we scoop the rook on h1, and even if White interposes by capturing our bishop, we have one more blow: the knight swings to f4 with a nasty check and then collects the d-pawn with the queen. It all works because White's queenside has never developed.

So we castle — the answer was yes. This is why we did the hard thinking in the opening's first ten moves: now the play is straightforward, and White is simply lost if the calculation holds. Once a queen takes c6 fails to that rook lift, White's position caves in; his queen goes from greatest asset to greatest liability — stranded offside on the queenside, unable to rejoin the game or defend the loose points scattered across the board. White can't even castle safely: a capture on d2 with a queen check on g5 rakes in the minor pieces, and our knight leaping to f4 hits g2 with mate ideas.

White tries a rook to g1. Now we shift from sharp tactics to simple technique. Our knight isn't really hanging — we can leave it on c6 — but why would we, when it has a dream square on d4? After the knight lands on d4 we've checked the ideas: if White captures our bishop, we recapture, and should the queen take on b4 our knight jumps to f3 forking the king and rook while unmasking a discovered hit on the d3 bishop. White can't hold everything together.

We take on d4, and there's nothing to fear — a bishop lunge to h6 at g7 is simply illegal, and there are no pieces near our king for White to attack. The one thing to avoid is pushing the f-pawn, which would allow a lateral back-rank mate. White's best try to stave off the doom is a bishop to e4, since it guards the sore f3 pawn; there's no easy way to hold f3 otherwise. Meanwhile we can pile up on the queenside with a rook to b8 or even set about trapping that stranded queen with a quiet a5.
White does defend with the bishop to e4. Now we just maximize — and the straightforward path is a rook to b8, bringing our last piece into the attack with tempo against the offside queen.

The rook swings to b8. From here it's take the bishop, take the b2 pawn, and our rook roars into the attack while White's queen is hopelessly stranded on a7 — it did its job snatching b7 and a7, but now it can't get home. When you sense the win is close, don't hunt only for mate: look for the move that wins material outright. A knight to c3 is the cleanest, hitting the rook and preparing tactics down the file. There are a dozen winning tries — a queen to h4, a knight to f4 — but the discipline is to choose simple, healthy moves and never blow it chasing a brilliancy: a flashy queen check that lets the king slip out can hand back the whole advantage. White is completely cooked and resigns.

But my recommendation slips through the cracks — the Nimzowitsch French: the knight to f3, developing as if nothing's wrong, letting Black wreck our pawn chain by taking on d4. It seems utterly counter-intuitive to allow that, even to sacrifice the d4 pawn, which is what we'll do.

Black develops the knight to c6. We keep developing as though Black exerts no pressure on d4. One common beginner mistake here is the bishop to b5 — not because it drops a piece, since after a queen-a5 check there's the knight to c3, but conceptually: the bishop on b5 is a paper tiger, and Black just blocks with the bishop to d7.

The best square for our bishop is d3, for several reasons. With a pawn on d4 like this, placing the bishop behind it is good practice: if Black castles kingside — the likeliest direction — we'll have a Greek-gift sacrifice ready.

They do, and we retreat the bishop to e2 — but we've PROVOKED c4, and with the centre relatively closed we can afford to move the same piece twice. What did provoking c4 achieve? It took the pressure off d4 — our chain is safe now — so we can focus on completing kingside development.

Black's queenside pawns look imposing, and b5 is actually a good move — but Black has bitten off more than she can chew, pushing all those pawns without piece support. We'll use OUR pawns, a very typical idea, to break down the whole chain.
We pressure both the c4 and b5 pawns at once: b3 hits c4, and we'll follow with a4 — classic pawn play to demolish Black's chain as fast as possible.

The bishop to a6 is powerful — our opponent tries to shield the chain with the minor pieces, but they're just not good at keeping a pawn chain intact.

And after d takes c4, capturing on c4, we've achieved exactly what we set out to do — a long-term, permanent weakness on c4. Step three has two parts: complete development and solidify our own chain. The solidifying move every French-with-White player knows is c3. Not the knight to c3 — the knight goes to d2 here, because the ultimate plan is to harass and win the c4 pawn. I like to castle kingside first, getting the king clear with no nasty checks on b4, then play c3.
So we castle first — safe, since Black has no good way to hit d4; the rook to d8 is likely at this level — then we follow with c3.

Instead Black plays f6. Note the knight can't take on e5 — our f3-knight guards it. Black tries to open the centre, but that's counterproductive when you're behind in development. This is a great moment for flexibility: our whole c3-then-knight-d2 scheme is set aside, because f6 changes everything. Who benefits when the centre opens? The better-developed side with fewer weaknesses — clearly us.
So we welcome it — e takes f6, capturing on f6: you want to open the centre? Thank you very much.

Black recaptures with the knight, capturing on f6 — and now the e-file opens onto a massive weakness on e6. Two weaknesses in Black's camp: the new one on e6 and the old one on c4. Put them together and you get the classy move, the queen to e2, hitting both pawns at once. A good alternative is simply the rook to e1 — e6 is the juicy pawn; win it and we mate soon. After the queen to e2, though, there's the nasty knight takes d4: knight takes d4, knight takes d4, queen takes d4, we grab e6 with check, Black plays the bishop to e7, and I'm not sure White has a crystal-clear finish.

So the more controlled move is the rook to e1, leaving the queen guarding d4. It's incredibly hard for Black to defend e6, and Black's lack of development costs her — a developed f8-bishop would let her castle.
Black just doesn't have time to develop. The king to f7 tries to defend e6, but it's futile — the king is a poor defender in these positions.
There's a rip move — the simple fork on g5, knocking the king back. The game's far from over, though: we've won a pawn but our queenside is still undeveloped, so we need accuracy.

Jobava players like to keep the tension with a move like the queen to d2. White plays d4. It's a bone-dry, equal position — White isn't fighting for anything, and sometimes you just accept that.

White plays c3. After ...d5 we reach a symmetrical structure where we're effectively playing the white side, a tempo up.

White develops the bishop to d3. Notice we held our own bishop back to see where his went — a subtle posturing, making the opponent show his cards first.

We play the bishop to g4 — no need to defend the e4-knight, our pawn supports it. This makes White waste a tempo retreating to e2, a small annoyance. The plan is patient: the knight comes to d7, pinning White's f3-knight to the queen, and we build pressure inch by inch.
White castles. You can't do everything at once — you pile on pressure by degrees, and small problems eventually coalesce into big ones.

node.idea: The reply c5 against the king's-pawn — the Sicilian. Today's choice is the Accelerated Dragon, a fast, clean setup and one of the friendliest gateways into the whole Sicilian family: less theory, clearly defined ideas, quick development.
White develops the king's knight to f3, the standard move against the Sicilian, eyeing the centre.
The queenside knight to c6 — the Accelerated move order. The plan from here is simple: trade in the centre, fianchetto, and get pieces out with tempo.
White strikes with the pawn to d4, the central break every Open Sicilian is built on.
We capture on d4, conceding a share of the centre for quick development and an open c-file to lean on later.
White recaptures with the knight, reaching the classic Open Sicilian structure.
Now the fianchetto — the pawn to g6, clearing the way for the bishop onto the long diagonal. Getting that bishop out fast is the whole point of the Accelerated.
White develops the queenside knight to c3, guarding e4 and looking toward d5.
The bishop settles on g7, aimed straight down the long diagonal at White's centre and queenside. Rapid, natural development is the accelerated dragon's calling card.
White develops the dark-squared bishop to e3, a natural square that supports the knight and readies queenside castling.
Our king's knight comes to f6, hitting e4 and finishing minor-piece development. Depending on White's next setup, we'll castle, play d6, or in some lines even strike with d5.
The bishop to c4 — a sharp Sozin-flavoured try that stares down f7. We simply carry on developing.
We castle, and note what we're deliberately NOT doing: pushing the pawn to d6 yet. Holding it back preserves maximum flexibility for what comes next.

The knight steps back to e2 — a poor choice, because it abandons the strong central d4-square and does nothing active. And here's a reflex worth burning in: whenever White keeps a bishop on e3, always keep one eye on it. There is a way to challenge White at once. We could play the calm d6 — perfectly fine — but if we want to be maximally testing, a sharper idea is waiting.
The knight jumps to g4, leaping at the bishop on e3. If the bishop moves, we get to hit f2 and b2 at the same time — and with the c-pawn already traded off, that double attack has real teeth.
White slides the bishop to g5 rather than the tempting retreat to d4, which would just drop the bishop. Now the second pattern to know is armed: the queen sortie.
The queen swings out to b6, forking the pawns on f2 and b2. It carries risk — our light-squared bishop still isn't out — but the pressure should tell.
White castles, choosing to hold f2 and let the other pawn go. A garden-variety double attack: one of the two pawns is going to fall.
We capture on b2. The key question before ever taking like this is always the same — can the queen be trapped? Here, no chance.

White chases with the rook to b1, and the queen simply steps to a3. That's the whole safety net: from b2 the queen had a3, and beyond it a5 and c5 — too many routes to be caught in a single move. That is exactly the check to run before snatching a pawn: list the queen's escapes, and ask whether any one move takes them all away.

White's best try — the knight leaps to d5, generating real pressure, so we must be careful. A warning too: the natural queen-back-to-d6 to threaten mate actually loses on the spot to the check on c7, which peels away the queen's own defender.

The knight comes back into the centre to e5 — retreating from a loose square, hitting the bishop, and centralising, all at once. And crucially the queen still guards e7 for now: if White probes with a rook to b3, the c5-square is always waiting for the queen.

White tucks the bishop back to b3, out of harm's way. Now we diagnose what's blocking full consolidation. We'd love to play d6 to free the light-squared bishop — but d6 cuts the queen's defence of e7 and drops that pawn. So d6 has to wait.

Instead we start kicking. The real problem is White's two strong pieces on d5 and g5, so we chase at least one of them off. The pawn to h6 first — the most flexible poke, keeping options open depending on where the bishop runs.
The bishop retreats to h4, staying on the pin.
We keep coming — the pawn to g5, chasing the bishop away entirely. This unburdens our position and lets us consolidate on our own terms.

The bishop drops to g3. Now d6 finally works — e7 is covered well enough. We could also try e6, but combining g6 and e6 leaves too many dark-square holes, so there's no rush to chase the d5-knight yet.

So the pawn to d6 at last — solid and freeing. And if White tries the knight to c7, there's simply no follow-up: the rook steps to b8 and nothing comes of it. That jump only bites if a rook were sitting on e8, which it isn't.
White plays the correct plan — the pawn to h4, prying open our king. This won't be an easy game.
We finally develop the light-squared bishop to g4. Honest admission: White's h4 is stronger than it first looks — this was underestimated.
White centralises the queen to d2 — a good move. Now we've got an interesting resource: the queen to a5, trying to force the queens off.

The queen to a5, offering the trade. There's a tactical wrinkle — the check on c7 — but calculate one step further: after that check the king goes to h7, and because we're then hitting both White's queen and the checking knight, the queens come off. We hand back the extra pawn, but the mating danger evaporates.
White declines and lifts the queen to e3 — music to the ears, because the c7-check no longer works: that knight is now tied to defending the queen.
So the queen to c5, again pressing for the exchange and eyeing White's queen.
White sidesteps to d2. No matter — our queen is beautifully centralised while White's is tied to the knight. That means we can get on with the plan: e6.
The pawn to e6, kicking the d5-knight. A strange, tense structure — the pawn-grab has led to a real fight, and if the knight retreats to e3 there's a very pretty resource waiting.
The knight goes to e3. And here's that resource — not a gimmick, it genuinely does something.

The bishop drops in to f3! It's untouchable thanks to the fork, and the point is plain: we're hitting the e4-pawn. With such a strong knight on e5 backing the operation, that pawn is hard to hold — normally a capture on c5 would break the pin, but the other knight just recaptures and the bishop stays immune.
White grabs on g5.
We have to recapture on g5 — otherwise our whole kingside is shattered.
White captures our centralised knight, the bishop landing on e5.
We recapture on e5 with the other knight — all according to plan.
The knight to g3, a good defensive try. Suddenly our f3-bishop could become a liability — if White's queen ever steps aside, the bishop can be taken. Time to think about shoring it up.

The pawn to g4 — solidifying the bishop, and more than that, preparing to sacrifice it: if White captures on f3, our knight recaptures and gets anchored by this very pawn. The deeper idea is to bring the dark-squared bishop to h6 and crank up the pressure.
White finds a very strong move — the queen to c1. And now our f3-bishop really is trapped.
We carry on with the plan — the bishop to h6, pinning the knight and pouring heat onto White's position. The f3-bishop is lost, so we roll with it and turn it into fuel.
White takes the bishop, a pawn recapturing on f3.

And now the instructive choice — most players would recapture with the knight, but we take with the pawn. This f3-pawn is a far more dangerous attacker: it jams White's position and becomes an anchor point for mating ideas. We're down a piece for two pawns, but White's king is the one in danger.
White unpins with the queen to e1. We have many ways to improve.
The king to h7 — stepping off the g-file so the rook can pour down it into the attack.

White cracks under the pressure — the knight to c4, which simply hangs itself. But the beautiful point is that we don't need to take it. The first thing to notice isn't the loose knight — it's that White's pawn on f2 is now pinned, so it no longer guards the knight.
So the in-between move — the rook to g8, threatening the crushing capture on g3 with check. Once that knight vanishes, White's king stands utterly alone.
White's king shuffles to h2. We keep our eyes on the bigger prize, not the loose knight on c4.
The knight to g4 with check — crushing.

The king to h3. Now don't drown in the sea of winning moves — plan properly. The real target is getting the queen over to the kingside, ideally to h6. What's in the way? Our own bishop. So move the bishop first.
But we don't bury the bishop uselessly — the bishop to f4 keeps it in the attack while clearing the queen's route via g5 to h6.
White pushes the pawn to e5. And here we spot an even faster finish — the knight crashes in on f2 with check.

node.idea: White plays a knight to c3. Which reply depends on your Sicilian: Najdorf players play d6, Accelerated Dragon players play a knight to c6.

As Accelerated Dragon players, it's easy — we play g6, and if d4 comes we take and transpose straight into an Accelerated Dragon.

And we fianchetto the bishop to g7 — our first Accelerated Dragon.

White plays a bishop to e3. The zen of this opening is to delay d6 — playing it early lets White transpose into the sharp mainline Dragon, and by holding off we deny White comfortable queenside castling.
So we develop the knight to f6 first, keeping the option to play d5 in one fell swoop.

White plays a3 — a sideline I've never seen, essentially a waste of time since we're not putting anything on b4. But we can't play d5 yet: before castling, a bishop to b5 pins our knight and threatens a capture on c6 and a bishop fork on e6.
So we castle kingside first — the rule of thumb is only play d5 after castling. Now we're ready to open the center and punish White for delaying.
White plays a bishop to c4 — and here's the center fork trick, a ubiquitous idea you cannot play the Accelerated without knowing. The precondition is a bishop on c4 (or, for Black, on c5).
We play a knight capture on e4 anyway — it looks like a blunder, but with the trick in hand it isn't.
White recaptures on e4, and we meet it with d5.
d5 re-forks the knight and bishop — that's where the name comes from — and we win the piece back. White can give the piece for a pawn, but here it isn't even easy for him to regain it.

So we simply recapture on c4 — now we're up a pawn.
White trades queens into an endgame.
We recapture on d8 — we'll still need good technique to finish in style.

White plays c3, closing off our bishop. With queens off, our king is safe — so no need to rush the c8 bishop out; the bigger fish is the b2 pawn. Our pawn on c4 deep-freezes it: b2 is backward with no path forward, a huge weakness on an open file.

tree.intro: Let's walk through King's Gambit vs Caro-Kann Defense — White plays the King's Gambit, Black answers with the Caro-Kann Defense. Watch how they meet.
tree.outro: That's how King's Gambit vs Caro-Kann Defense plays out.

node.idea: We meet the king's pawn with c6 — the Caro-Kann.
White claims the full centre with d4.
We strike back at the centre with d5 — the heart of the Caro-Kann.
White pushes past with e5 — the Advance Variation, locking the centre and banking on space.

Here's the whole reason the Caro exists: unlike the French, we get to develop this light-squared bishop OUTSIDE the pawn chain, to f5, before we ever shut it in with e6 — and that's exactly what we've done. White answers with f4, grabbing more central space, but it's not a good move: it curbs the development of White's own light bishop and it weakens his king.
The proper reply is e6 — White has over-committed his pawns while lagging in development.

White develops the bishop to d3. Since this is our first Advance Caro, here's the rationale. The centre is CLOSED, and a closed centre is built of pawn chains — our black pawns form one chain, and d4 with e5 is White's chain. The side with more levers, more ability to attack and undermine the OTHER side's chain, is the side holding the initiative — and the whole point of the Caro is that Black is that side. White's compensation is space; those two things balance out. And right now we don't want to surrender this prime parking spot on f5 so easily — we trade it on OUR terms.
Trading on our own terms means: when this bishop comes off, we want to replace it with a KNIGHT. So the typical move is the knight to h6 — and if White takes on f5, we recapture with the knight.
White develops the knight to f3. Why do we want our knight to reach f5? To pressure d4. So the question becomes how we keep piling onto that pawn.
We play c5 — hitting the base of White's pawn chain, and at the same time opening the c6 square for our knight.
White trades, capturing on f5.
We recapture with the knight, capturing on f5 — and now we have TWO attackers bearing on the d4 pawn.
White castles. Now we could grab d4 at once, but to play it cleanly there's a subtlety worth a second — and note White can also take on c5, which we'll deal with.

Rather than snatch d4 immediately, we play the knight to c6 first — the more flexible move, since we want it on the board regardless. The queen to b6 is also possible, but we hold it in reserve: if White plays c3, THEN the queen to b6 becomes strong.
White plays c3, showing his intent to prop up d4.

Now the clean way is to take on d4 first and then play the queen to b6, winning the pawn — and in a real game that's what I'd do. But I want to show a beautiful idea, so I play the queen to b6 first, hoping he grabs a pawn.
White plays b3, refusing to walk into it.
He won't allow the trick, so we simply take, capturing on d4 — there's a lot to unpack in this Advance.

White recaptures, capturing on d4. This is a critical pawn: it's the link that breaks up his chain, and with two of our pieces attacking it against a single defender, it's falling — and his whole position starts to crumble.
The knight from c6 takes, capturing on d4 — we've won the pawn and reached the decisive stage: up material, with a protected passed pawn on d5.
White plays the king to h1 — a good move, sidestepping a discovered-check threat.
We ask what we haven't done yet, and develop with the bishop to c5 — a great move. The h5 push was also good, but we save it; g4 would have been White's best, though I don't expect it.
White takes our knight, capturing on d4 — a mistake; now he collapses. The only question is what we recapture with.
We recapture with the bishop, capturing on d4 — the right choice. White's rook is now in trouble, and the game is essentially over: he's losing it.

White finds g4. Here's a common trap — tunnel vision. After a move like the bishop to d4, many players automatically snatch the rook on a1. But look wider: taking on a1 gives up our knight, so White gets a knight back for the rook — a real chunk of material. So we do NOT grab the rook immediately.

And not the knight to e3 either — White just takes it, and then our bishop, which we've assigned the vital task of winning the rook, gets distracted defending. Instead we simply drop the knight back to e7. The point isn't to activate it; we're after far greener pastures — the rook. White's best is the knight to c3, cutting his losses to just the knight.
White does find the knight to c3, and we take it, capturing on c3 — good defence, but we're winning the rook.
White saves the rook to b1. Now — White's king is very weak: the move g4 has opened a direct avenue toward it.

We exploit that avenue with d4 — a move doing several jobs at once: it shelters our bishop on c3, advances our passed pawn, and prepares the queen to c6, setting up a discovered check. It also opens the path for our e7-knight to reroute via d5 and even into e3 when we're ready.

node.idea: f3 — the Fantasy Variation. Instead of the usual moves, we bolster e4 with the f-pawn and dare Black to try to punish the loosened kingside.
Black develops with a knight to d7 — and I'll be honest, I've never seen it here. It isn't a top move; I'd call it an inaccuracy: passive, and it does nothing to contest the center.

So we close it down with e5. I want to give you a broad tour of a closed-center position — a lot of players feel lost when the center locks, as if they're just shuffling pieces. In truth these are some of the richest games in chess, because they force play on the flanks, where the most beautiful and tactical ideas live. Our next job is to reinforce both links of the d4-e5 chain, because Black will attack it with pawns.
c5 hits the base of our chain — a classic French break. Black can also come from the other side with f6, which is exactly why I like f4.
c3, a no-brainer, propping up d4. We absolutely don't want the chain to dissolve this early with no pieces out — that chain is the only thing standing between us and disaster.

The knight belongs on f3; a knight to e2 would be awkward and would bury the light-squared bishop. Black's queen to c7 is a bit pointless — it doesn't even threaten a capture on d4, since we recapture and the c1 bishop is guarded by our own queen. So we keep developing, and the move order is flexible.

I'll bring the bishop to d3 first, since we're lagging in development and haven't moved a minor piece — and it also keeps the knight-to-e2 option alive, which is far more palatable once the bishop is already out.
Black plays e6, and we keep everything as flexible as possible — with the opponent playing so unambitiously, we can leave many developing paths open.
Now f4 — the maximally ambitious, textbook move, grabbing space and taking the fight to the opponent.
Black plays g6. The c1 bishop starts complaining that it's staring at its own pawn, but it has fine squares on e3 or d2 — not every piece has to climb Everest at once.
On e3 the bishop actually does a great job further supporting the chain, which we want rock-solid. But first, the knight to f3 — let's get the pieces we know how to place out.

Black's knight goes to e7, heading for f5 to press d4 in true French fashion. Don't be tempted by g4 to stop it — that's far too cavalier with so little developed. After g4, h5 is a classic response: we can't answer h3, Black captures on g4, and the h1 rook hangs, so g4 hands Black a huge f5 outpost instead of denying one.

So the bishop to e3 — and the subtlety is that when the knight lands on f5, our bishop slides back to f2. Castle first and that retreat to e3 is no longer available; the small developmental detail decides how smoothly the game runs.
The knight comes to f5, and the bishop drops to f2, first overprotecting the d4 pawn and, much later, eyeing a route into Black's position.
A bishop maneuver to h4 and f6 is a common infiltration, especially against a fianchetto with a bishop fianchettoed to g7.
We castle and keep developing. The h5 push is typical for this structure.

h5 does prevent g4, but it creates major dark-square weaknesses — notice the outpost on g5. That doesn't mean we leap there now; a knight to g5 lets Black trade and fill the holes. Later, though, g5 becomes a transit square, and a plan of trading on f5 and swinging the bishop to h4 hands our queen a swarm of juicy kingside outposts. With the center closed we have time — the position simply doesn't change fast.

A knight to a3 is a dead-end after a6, so instead the b1 knight goes to d2 — toward the center, going nowhere in particular yet, a Frankfurt-airport move you never regret. Remember, closed positions offer two broad plans: arrange your pieces to blast the center open, or maneuver on a flank.

Black plays a queen to b6. Here's our plan: rip the whole thing open and bank on our more active pieces handling the chaos better. Not a capture on c5 — that just hands Black space and the e3 square. Instead c4, building a pawn box that guarantees the center will open, perhaps after first eliminating Black's only active piece with a capture on f5.

c4 it is — and we can delay the capture on f5, playing it a little later. And we're not afraid of losing b2: when you've castled on the opposite wing a single b-pawn almost never matters, and here our queenside stays intact — Black can't unravel it the way a b2-then-c3 collapse would.

The queen grabs b2, but it creates no threats and doesn't stop our central agenda. Trying to trap it with a queen to a4 and a rook to b1 fails to a strong resource, and we lack the queenside firepower anyway — so we keep our focus in the center and press to open it.

We start with a move we know is good — capturing on d5. If Black doesn't recapture, the pawn marches to d6 and it's horrific for him, so he'll take back, and then a capture on f5 to wreck his structure is the idea.
Black recaptures on d5, and we should be tempted to grab the knight on f5 — giving up our light-square control hurts, but it's a price well worth paying.
So we capture on f5, taking the knight, while we still can, trading our good bishop to shatter Black's kingside pawns.
Black recaptures with the g-pawn, and now we complete the opening of the center.

We finish it with a capture on c5 — the center is now fully open, so we shift from luxurious positional play to hunting tactics. Black still hasn't developed his queenside, and we've invested a pawn, so we must hit the gas.
Black recaptures on c5. Only a couple of moves stand between him and consolidating that extra pawn, so we accelerate — and a bishop to d4 catches my eye, x-raying the rook.

The bishop to d4 hits the queen, centralizes beautifully, and prepares an e6 discovery against the rook — good as a plan and good as a plain developing move. It also shoos away that b2 queen, which was cramping our coordination.
Black shuffles the queen to a3, but our reply to almost anything here is e6 — and our opponent is defending this fantastically, making us work.
e6 is nearly automatic: without it, Black plants a knight into e6 and keeps the center closed.
Black plays a rook to g8 — and that, I think, is the decisive mistake.
Because now, without a second thought, we capture on f7, dragging the king out into the open.

The king is forced to f7 — f6 was the only survival try. Now the firepower tells: a knight to e5 with check, and lines flow, though a queen grab on h5 with check isn't yet mate because the king slips to d8.
A knight to e5 with check. Black could try the king to g6, using the king itself as a defender, but there's no reason to overcomplicate — the knight to e5 is clean.

The king walks out to e6. This looks like hara-kiri for Black. One pitfall for us is a rook to e1 — there's a knight jump to e4 in reply, and if the king ever steps to d6 a knight to c4 forks king and queen. No need for any of that: the simplest move is to capture the h-pawn, not for the pawn but to route the queen toward f7.

The queen takes h5, Black defends with a rook to f8, and the queen checks from h6 — the whole point being to prevent a bishop to f6. Compare your checks: two similar-looking checks rarely do the same job.
The rook is driven to f6, and remember — even mid-attack you're allowed to win material. Players fixate on delivering mate; here the rook sits under the bishop's x-ray.
A queen to g7 — using the weakness of Black's king to go after his pieces, because a king so exposed forces the defenders onto vulnerable squares.
Black finds the only move, a queen to b4, holding things together; a queen check on g8 and the king to d6 leaves us with a beautiful win to find.

A knight to f3 is what I like — it gives away nothing, prepares a knight to g5, and safely defends the bishop. A resilient defender makes you work, but at most levels the position collapses in a couple of moves.
Crucially, we've sacrificed nothing — it's plus eleven. If Black plays a knight to e4 to take the sting out of a knight to g5, the top computer move is a wonderfully quiet one.
Just a rook to c1 — bringing a piece into the attack and cutting the king off from its escape. These quiet inclusions are the moves people won't make when attacking, yet they decide the game.
Against a bishop to d7 we simply play a rook to c7.
The rook to c7 — its added presence overwhelms Black's defense.
Black tries a rook to d8, and the engine's move is striking.
A knight to f7.
After the rook takes it, a queen to e5 is checkmate — a pretty little concept, everything protected, completely one-sided.
